question.text: What is the difference between a 'swap' and other derivative types?

answer.text: A swap is an agreement to exchange cash flows over multiple future dates according to a formula — it is essentially a series of forward contracts bundled together
A swap is the same as a futures contract but traded OTC
A swap only involves exchanging equity shares between two parties
Swaps are only used in commodity markets for physical delivery

explanation.text: The Logic: NISM Series IV page 94 defines a swap as an agreement between two parties to exchange future cash flows according to an agreed formula, and describes swaps as broadly a series of forward contracts. Page 91 lists forwards, futures, swaps and options as the four basic derivative types across asset classes, and Series I pages 40-41 confirm that currency/FX swaps share the same cash-flow-exchange structure. The Trap: Swaps are not the same as futures — they are typically OTC, customised and involve multiple cash-flow exchanges rather than a single settlement. They also exist across all major underlying asset classes (interest rate, currency, equity and commodity) and are not restricted to equities or to commodity physical delivery. Note: The "series of forwards" description and the cash-flow definition are taken directly from Series IV page 94; the cross-asset coverage is supported by Series IV page 91 and Series I pages 40-41.
